extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers, and policymakers interested in doxing, privacy, and cybercrime
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes what doxing is, common techniques and harms, defensive/anti-doxing advice, and country-by-country legal/regulatory treatments and penalties for doxing-related conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of doxing
rubrics_metrics.description: "Doxing or doxxing is the act of publicly providing personally identifiable information about an individual or organization, usually via the Internet and without their consent, and or with the intention of harassing or causing distress to the victim."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains both aggregation of information from public sources and publication of previously private information obtained by criminal or fraudulent means (hacking, social engineering). Notes the term's negative connotation when used as revenge or privacy violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation of public information vs illicit acquisition
rubrics_metrics.description: The aggregation and provision of previously published material is generally legal, though it may be subject to laws concerning stalking and intimidation; publication of previously private information obtained through criminal or otherwise fraudulent means (such as hacking and social engineering) is distinguished and often unlawful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page highlights that legality can turn on how information was obtained and the surrounding intent; examples and historical context (forums, hacker culture) are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent and motivation as a legal/ethical element
rubrics_metrics.description: Doxing frequently involves intent to harass, intimidate, extort, punish, or hold someone publicly accountable; motivations include online shaming, extortion, vigilantism, exposing harmful behavior, embarrassing, threatening, or cyberstalking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that some instances may be justified (e.g., revealing harmful behavior) only if the doxing aligns with public interest; intent (to intimidate/harass) is central in many legal definitions described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques for obtaining and weaponizing dox
rubrics_metrics.description: Common techniques include aggregating public records and social media, hack‑based exfiltration, social engineering, and malware-assisted theft (doxware).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page describes how harvested data may be used for account takeover, extortion, or to support harassment actions like swatting and in-person harassment; dating apps and intimate-partner contexts are noted as vectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doxware (malware-enabled doxing/extortion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Doxware is a cryptovirology attack that steals a victim's data and threatens to publish it unless a fee is paid; it is the converse of ransomware.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes the cryptovirology/game-theory origins (Young & Yung) and contrasts doxware with cryptoviral extortion/ransomware where access to data is denied rather than threatened with publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-doxing harassment methods and harms
rubrics_metrics.description: After being doxed, victims may face in-person harassment, fake signups, unwanted deliveries, bombarding an address with letters, swatting (false emergency reports that summon armed police), threats, and psychological harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Swatting is highlighted as illegal and dangerous; penalties for swatting and general ramifications (death threats, reputational harm) are discussed; examples from recent incidents are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-doxing protective measures (individual-level guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical mitigations include 'Google yourself, lock yourself down, make it harder to access information about you.' Institutions (e.g., universities) and privacy/cybersecurity organizations provide guidance and services to reduce exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References UC Berkeley guidance and EFF recommendations; advice is presented as general best-practice steps rather than guaranteed protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Australia: criminalization under Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024
rubrics_metrics.description: In 2024 Australia introduced legislation (Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024, effective 10 December 2024) that introduced criminal penalties for doxxing, including provisions making doxing punishable by jail time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes bipartisan political support and that the reform responded to the large-scale leak of personal data of over 600 Australians; situates the law as a recent national-level criminalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Austria: anti‑stalking and cyber‑mobbing framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Austria passed an anti-stalking law in 2006 and made cyber-mobbing a criminal offense in 2016; as of end of 2024 doxing is not a specific offense but these laws are used in online violence cases and EU law (GDPR) applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page indicates prosecutors apply existing statutes to doxing incidents rather than a single dedicated doxing statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mainland China: Regulations on the Ecological Governance of Online Information Content (2020)
rubrics_metrics.description: From March 1, 2020, Chinese regulations clarify that users and producers of online information content services and platforms must not engage in online violence, doxing, deep forgery, data fraud, account manipulation and other illegal activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treats doxing as part of a broader regulatory regime governing online content and platform obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hong Kong: statutory offense and penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: As of 2021, Hong Kong criminalized doxing defined as releasing private or non-public information for the purposes of 'threatening, intimidation, harassment or to cause psychological harm'; convicted persons face up to 5 years' imprisonment and a fine of HK$1,000,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides the statutory definition and maximum penalties; emphasizes the strong criminal sanction in Hong Kong law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Germany: Section 126a 'endangering dissemination of personal data' and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Since September 2021 Germany criminalized the endangering dissemination of personal data (Section 126a StGB); publishing freely accessible data can be punishable (up to two years or a fine) and publishing non‑freely accessible data up to three years; the act must be suitable and, under the circumstances, intended to expose the person to a crime or other unlawful act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes statutory exception referencing Section 86 Paragraph 4—acts are not punishable if socially appropriate (civic education, art, science, reporting on current events or history).

rubrics_metrics.name: Netherlands: felony for sharing personal data for intimidation (effective Jan 1, 2024)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dutch law makes it a felony to share personal data with the intent of intimidation, harassment or work‑hindering; carries a maximum penalty of two years' prison or a fine (increased by one third when targeted at certain public figures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes legislative history and effective date (1 January 2024); emphasizes intent to intimidate as an element and enhanced penalties for targeting certain public figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Russia: Article 137 'Invasion of Personal Privacy'
rubrics_metrics.description: Russian law criminalizes public sharing of personal information using mass media, Internet, or public events; penalties range from fines and compulsory/corrective labor to imprisonment of up to two years and possible deprivation of rights; copying information and obtaining it illegally are separate offenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies a broad set of punishments and that derivative offences (illicit obtaining/copying) are also punishable.

rubrics_metrics.name: South Korea: Act on Promotion of Information and Communications Network Utilization (Article 49)
rubrics_metrics.description: South Korea's Article 49 prohibits unlawful collection and dissemination of private information such as full name, birth date, address, likeness, and any other information sufficient to identify a person when viewed in summation, regardless of intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice ambiguity around 'unlawful collection' leads prosecutors to rely on other provisions (e.g., Article 44 prohibiting insults/defamation) that may carry harsher sentences; statute enacted partly in response to celebrity suicides from cyberbullying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spain: Criminal Code articles 197–201 (discovery and revelation of secrets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spanish Criminal Code punishes discovering secrets or violating privacy (seizing papers, intercepting communications, using technical devices) with prison sentences of one to four years and fines; disseminating such data to third parties carries higher penalties (two to five years), with aggravated penalties for revealing ideology, religion, health, sexual life, underage or disabled victims, or if done for economic profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also criminalizes dissemination of images obtained with consent in private settings if disclosure seriously undermines privacy; penalties are especially severe when familial relationships exist or victims are underage or disabled.

rubrics_metrics.name: United States: limited federal remedies and state-level variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal statutes potentially relevant (Interstate Communications Statute and Interstate Stalking Statute) are underinclusive or rarely enforced (Interstate Communications criminalizes explicit threats; Interstate Stalking is rarely enforced). Several states (notably California and Colorado) have specific state laws making doxing illegal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarly critique that federal laws are inadequate; remarks that weak U.S. data-privacy regimes and data brokers make personal information widely accessible and contribute to doxing opportunities; notes swatting and political weaponization in recent years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal remedies and enforcement variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Across jurisdictions, legal remedies for victims of doxing vary widely: some countries have dedicated statutes, others apply existing stalking/defamation/privacy laws, and enforcement intensity differs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page repeatedly emphasizes that outcomes depend on local law, available evidence of intent or illicit acquisition, and prosecutorial priorities; scholars note gaps in deterrence when laws are underinclusive or rarely applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for when doxing may be treated as socially appropriate or protected
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain legal regimes carve out exceptions where dissemination of personal data is not punishable if 'socially appropriate'—e.g., serves civic education, defense against unconstitutional efforts, art or science, research, teaching, reporting on current events or history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Germany's statutory exception (referring to Section 86 Paragraph 4) is cited as an example; such exceptions create a balancing test between privacy and public interest.
